responses.mission_1.search:
open	bfs	succeeded	0.001602572000138025	928 	30	13.5	13.5	1
open	astar	succeeded	0.0023997070002224064	700	  111	13.5	13.5	1
The length is equal with 13.5. A* examined less cells with 700 while BFS examined 928. BFS is a FIFO queue so explores uniformly out and does not go towards the direction of the goal and goes in all directions until it finds the goal. A* is a heap that prototiles less cost and has heuristics that leads it closer to the goal.
responses.mission_1.failure: IDDFS has has a resource_limit status and expanded a lot more than the DFS and BFS and it couldn't find a path to the goal. This is because IDDFS keeps rerunning from depth 0 each time so it would expand a lot while DFS and BFS visits a node once. For the 4 unreachable cases, BFS, DFS, and A* all have no_path status and IDDFS has resource_limit status. The difference between no_path and resource_limit is that no_path is that the algorithm stops because it knows that it went through all possible paths and can not reach the goal. resource_limit is that the algorithm keeps expanding and reaches some number of expands before the guardrail stops it from doing even more expansions.
responses.mission_2.prediction: A* will finish sooner compared to DFS because A* goes on in the direction closes to heading to the goal so it will not make unnecessary routes while DFS will find a route but the route might not be optimized.
responses.mission_2.performance: A* has  success status distance_m of 23.799087360191233	and elapsed_s of 88.96600000000001.DFS has status of controller_failed distance_m of 31.53589499690114 and elapsed_s of 145.08599999999998. The results supported my prediction. The plot showed that DFS was doing zigzags when it could have just went down like in A*. I was surprised that DFS did not complete the route and stopped in the middle of its route.
responses.mission_2.choice: I would choose nav2 for a delivery plan. The status is succeeded for both maps. Constrained elapsed_s is 74.454 which is the quickest, open elapsed_s is 35.5 which is also the quickest. Chose it over RRT because it controller failed on the constrained map. The advantages that mapper most for my choice is that it should be fastest route and doesn't have errors.
responses.mission_3.prediction: Repulsion strength changes how much the robot should move away from the repulsion zone.  Influence distance (m) changes the area of the repulsion zone around the person. Refinement step (m) is how much the robot should move on its next step.
responses.mission_3.comparison: The largest minimum_person_clearance_m is the baseline RRT. All the RRT navigation had a personal_space_s of 0. Social 1 and 2 have slightly less minimum_person_clearance_m compared to the baseline. The wider spacing costed more distance but surprisingly it costed slightly less time. Social 2 elapsed_s is 43.28 and distance_m is 11.582686735757513. Social 2 elapsed_s is 43.594 and distance_m is 11.592291109948228. Baseline elasped_s is 43.956 and distance_m is 11.502098268502493.
responses.mission_3.recommendation:
I would keep any of the RRT navigation because it takes, traveled less distance, takes less time and avoids the person more. Static person trials do not test the robot behavior if a person is moving in its planned route. 
Social 2 RRT status is succeeded, elapsed_s is 43.594, distance_m is 11.592291109948228 and minimum_person_clearance_m is 1.7157979088470554.
Social 2 A* stus is succeeded, elapsed_s is 46.366, distance_m  is 13.164319817672448, and minimum_person_clearance_m  is 0.7249049164181913.
responses.final.synthesis: A route suitable for a robot sharing space with people is that the robot should find an efficient pathing so it doesn't make the people around them confused on its pathing like the pathing of DFS and that it should also avoid people so that it doesn't crash into them. IDDFS does not seem like a good searching algorithm since it keeps repeating searches at increasing depth limits and DFS does not guarantee the best route. We would also need to test out the searching algorithms first because it may cause errors like controller failing where on the constrained map RRT has a controller error.
responses.final.course_reflection: I found it interesting how different search algorithms can produce different results even when given the same map. Seeing the map of how the robot moves in the maps made it more clear on the algorithms benefits and drawbacks. I was surprised that IDDFS used so many resources on small map and that DFS could find a route that made the controller fail. Same with RRT on constrained map.
